title: 2010 IMO Problem 3
statement:
Find all functions \(g \colon \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) such that
\[ \left( g(m)+n \right)\left( g(n)+m \right) \]
is always a perfect square.

solutions.text:
For \(c \ge 0\), the function \(g(n) = n+c\) works; we prove this is the only possibility.

First, the main point of the problem is that:

Claim.
 We have \(g(n) \equiv g(n') \pmod p \implies n \equiv n' \pmod p\).

Proof.
 Pick a large integer \(M\) such that
 \[ \nu_p(M+g(n)), \quad \nu_p(M+g(n')) \quad \text{are both odd}. \]
 (It's not hard to see this is always possible.)
 Now, since each of
 \[\begin{aligned}
 \left( M + g(n) \right)&\left( n + g(M) \right) \\
 \left( M + g(n') \right)&\left( n' + g(M) \right)
 \end{aligned}\]
 is a square, we get \(n \equiv n' \equiv -g(M) \pmod p\).

This claim implies that

• The numbers \(g(n)\) and \(g(n+1)\) differ by \(\pm 1\) for any \(n\), and

• The function \(g\) is injective.

It follows \(g\) is a linear function with slope \(\pm 1\), hence done.
